beat: Hardened communications and infrastructure — AT&T Long Lines hardened microwave and coaxial plant, the AT&T 'Project Office' troposcatter chain, AUTOVON switching, Western Union's hardened government microwave, and the records-storage / data-centre typology that inherited these buildings after divestiture. First discovery sweep, cycle 1.
method_notes:
WHAT I DID. Approximately twenty WebSearch passes against the general index, working outward from four seeds: (1) the AT&T Long Lines corpus (long-lines.net, Garrett Fuller, computer.rip, FAS L-4 page); (2) the 'Project Office' literature (coldwar-c4i.net, CLUI Land Use Database, Wikipedia); (3) local and trade press covering land-use proceedings at surviving sites (Loudoun Times-Mirror, Loudoun Now, Indy Week, Data Center Dynamics); and (4) the commercial afterlife of these buildings (Vital Records Inc., InfoBunker, brokerage listings, Amherst College / Five Colleges).

WHAT WAS BLOCKED. WebFetch is effectively unavailable on this beat. I attempted en.wikipedia.org, long-lines.net and coldwar-ct.com and all three returned EGRESS_BLOCKED from the network proxy. I did not attempt .gov hosts, which the brief states are blocked. This means: I never reached wireless2.fcc.gov (ASR/ULS), never reached a county recorder or assessor, never reached Loudoun County's land-development records, never reached Albemarle County's permit viewer, never reached NARA/CREST/DTIC/GovInfo, never reached USGS HTMC. Those are precisely the corpora BES §7.1 designates canonical for EXIST, LOCATE, CONTROL, HARDEN and FUNCTION on this typology.

THE CONSEQUENCE, STATED PLAINLY. Not one observation below resolved to bytes. Every source row is receipt_state = UNRESOLVED-UNREACHABLE, receipt_class = R-NONE, and therefore tier V0 — arithmetically inert on every condition (§2.2, §2.4). V is empty for every proposition in this file. CAP-5 would cap everything at F; but the Search Completeness Index is 0 or near 0 on every proposition, because none of the canonical corpora were searched with a receipt, so §9.4 step 2 returns X before F is reached. **Every proposed_band in this file is therefore X — NOT ASSESSED, and that is the correct BES v0.2 output for this sweep, not a failure of it.** Where the record as described in search snippets would plausibly support a different band once receipts resolve, I say so in the proposition's `assessment` field as a conditional, never as a grade. Treat the conditionals as work orders, not as findings.

WHAT I SAW vs WHAT I INFER. I saw search-result titles, URLs and the search tool's prose summaries of page contents. I did not see any page. Where a summary states that a page says X, I have evidence that a summary asserts X — one further remove from the page, and two removes from whatever the page cites. Several summaries in this session were themselves synthesised across multiple results, which means I cannot always attribute a specific sentence to a specific URL. I have flagged this in `what_it_actually_shows` per source and have not attributed a quotation to a page unless the summary tied them together explicitly.

IDENTIFIERS — THE HIGHEST-RISK ITEM. Three FCC Antenna Structure Registration numbers surfaced in a summary of Garrett Fuller's blog (Brinktown MO 1005484, Dover MO 1010168, Lawrenceton MO 1005501), and two AT&T CLLI codes (HGTWMDQ0010 for the Hagerstown Project Office, LSBGVA05 for the Leesburg / Short Hill Mountain Project Office), plus one Loudoun County application number (CMPT-2016-0001) and one later one (CMPT-2020-0005). **I have not resolved any of them.** They are format-plausible and they came from a summary of a third-party page, which is exactly the F-05 canary condition: a well-formed identifier is cheap to produce and expensive to check. They are recorded here as LEADS for the acquisition queue under §2.7, not as citations, and no proposition in this file leans on any of them. If any fails to resolve at the FCC or at Loudoun County, that is a measured confabulation event and should be recorded against this run.

COORDINATES — DELIBERATELY WITHHELD. I have no resolved coordinate for any candidate. I could produce town or landform centroids from model memory, but under §3.1 that is an interpretation asserted by a fleet agent and therefore T5, and under §10.3 a precise pin manufactured from imprecise evidence is the register performing citogenesis on itself. Every `location` object below carries a verbal description at the granularity the sources actually support (county, named landform, named road) and no lat/lon. That verbal granularity is enough for the next agent to run a point-in-polygon against HTMC or a parcel query; a fabricated decimal degree is not.

RECALL, NOT CORROBORATION. Per §5.0: this fan-out improves recall only. If another agent on another beat returns the same Project Office chain, that is the same indexed corpus found twice, not a second witness. I have made no use of my own thoroughness as evidence.

WHAT I COULD NOT ESTABLISH. (a) No federal primary record — CREST, DTIC, GAO, NARA, MILCON — naming the AT&T 'Project Office' programme was found in the general index. Under the expected-record table this absence is close to uninformative for a 1960s programme run through a common carrier under a classified contract, but it does mean the entire COG reading of these five stations currently rests on one named researcher's stated inference. (b) I could not determine whether the AT&T Project Offices were federally funded, cost-shared, or built entirely on AT&T capital — which is the single fact that would most change the CONTROL and FUNCTION analysis. (c) I could not establish per-site hardening class for any Long Lines building; the published hardening figures are network-wide design criteria, not instance specifications. (d) I could not verify the Peters Mountain $61M permit claim to a permit number.

candidates.name: AT&T Long Lines "Project Office" chain — five hardened mid-Atlantic troposcatter stations
candidates.era: Built late 1950s to mid-1960s; terminal stations reported in service 1963 (Hagerstown) and 1966 (Chatham); troposcatter links reported out of service by the 2000s; two stations reportedly still AT&T-operated.
candidates.jurisdiction: Multi-state: Washington County MD; Loudoun County VA; Albemarle County VA; Buckingham County VA; Chatham County NC

location.description: A north–south chain of five hardened stations running from the Bear Pond Mountains northwest of Hagerstown, Maryland, through Short Hill Mountain in western Loudoun County, Virginia; Peters Mountain roughly 16 miles east of Charlottesville, Virginia; Spears Mountain roughly 11 miles west of the town of Buckingham, Virginia; to a site off Big Hole Road in Chatham County, North Carolina, south of Chapel Hill.
location.basis: Verbal placement only, taken from search summaries of the CLUI Land Use Database and coldwar-c4i.net. No coordinate was resolved in this session and none is asserted. The landform names above are the strongest locators the sources supply and are sufficient to drive a parcel or HTMC query.

propositions.statement: AT&T built, in the late 1950s–1960s, a programme of five nuclear-hardened troposcatter communications stations in the mid-Atlantic, internally referred to as 'Project Offices', whose nature AT&T has never publicly described beyond calling them 'central facilities'.
propositions.assessment: The programme's existence as a named, bounded set is the best-supported thing on this beat. Three sources that do not obviously copy one another — Albert LaFrance's coldwar-c4i.net, the CLUI Land Use Database, and Jon Elliston's 2000 Indy Week reporting — independently describe a small chain of AT&T-built hardened tropo stations, and CLUI and LaFrance agree on the count of five. Nothing I saw is a primary record. Conditional: if a Bell System route/plant document or an AT&T corporate history naming the programme resolves, PROG plausibly reaches B; if only the compilations resolve, PROG is capped at C by CAP-1 because CLUI most likely descends from LaFrance.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net ATT_Project index — 'Five nuclear-hardened, secure communications stations were built by AT&T in the mid-1960s in sparsely-populated areas of the mid-Atlantic region'
CLUI Land Use Database — Short Hill Mountain entry describes 'one of five similar facilities in the mid-Atlantic region known as Project Offices'
Wikipedia 'Project Offices' — AT&T 'has chosen not to disclose the exact nature of business conducted at Project Offices, describing them only as central facilities'
Elliston, Indy Week, 13 Dec 2000, 'Big Hole, Deep Secret' — investigative reporting on one member of the set
undercutting: No federal primary record naming the programme was found in the general index. Under the ERP table this is near-uninformative (see expected_records), so it is listed as a gap rather than scored as a negative.
AT&T's own refusal to describe the facilities is consistent both with a classified federal mission and with ordinary common-carrier reticence about critical network plant — it does not discriminate.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A named programme of five stations is not by itself diagnostic of anything beyond 'AT&T built five stations'. What discriminates is the described feature set — earth-covered buildings, drive-through decontamination bays, blast valves, helipads, physical security beyond conventional AT&T practice — none of which a routine microwave relay carries. That feature set is D2-ish IF an instance-level record confirms it. Today it is asserted by compilations only.

propositions.statement: Five substantial earth-covered subsurface structures exist at the five named locations.
propositions.assessment: Scope is CLASS here, not INSTANCE — this proposition is about the set. Per §2.4 class evidence cannot certify any individual hilltop, and the individual site entries below carry their own EXIST. What can be said: multiple independent site-visit-based compilations, at least one peer-reviewed article, at least one investigative newspaper piece, and a county land-use proceeding in which AT&T applied to build ON TOP of an existing underground building, all place substantial subsurface structures at these coordinates. Conditional: individually these would likely reach B–A once county parcel records and USGS HTMC temporal stacks are pulled, because a 1960s excavation of this scale leaves deed, assessment and cartographic traces that are X3 expected records.
supporting: CLUI entries for Short Hill Mountain, Chatham, Peters Mountain Road and Buckingham each describe an underground building
Loudoun County commission permit proceeding 2016 in which AT&T sought to build a 160,000 sq ft aboveground structure adjacent to 'its already-existing underground facility'
coldwar-c4i.net per-site pages describing earth-covered buildings with drive-through entrance-decontamination areas
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A buried building is on the universal-D0 list — limestone mines, sewer works and cold storage all produce one. What lifts it above D0 for this set is not the hole but the drive-through decontamination bay and blast valves, which no mundane alternative for a telephone relay produces. That distinction is exactly why EXIST and HARDEN must be graded apart.

propositions.statement: The Project Offices served a continuity-of-government function beyond their AUTOVON switching role — specifically, sheltering or supporting federal officials in a nuclear emergency.
propositions.assessment: This is the load-bearing claim on the whole beat and it is the weakest. Its origin is a single named researcher's explicitly hedged inference. LaFrance writes, in the summaries I saw, that AUTOVON switching 'was probably not the station's primary mission', that the AUTOVON equipment was 'installed to serve another activity housed at the sites', and that it is 'likely' and 'most likely' that the stations supported a classified COG programme and 'may have served' as a relocation site. Wikipedia, CLUI and the downstream popular press restate the conclusion with the hedges stripped. That is the citogenesis pattern the register exists to name. Conditional: even with full receipts, this cannot exceed E under CAP-2b unless a verified instance-scope CLAIM-PROPERTY record appears, because every current support is either place-property (the building has a helipad) or is the compiler's inference.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net — hedged inference that the stations supported a classified COG programme
Greenbrier bunker switchboard reportedly labelled 'CHATAM' and 'HGRSTOWN' — a physical artefact inside a declassified, publicly toured federal COG facility naming two members of this chain
Wikipedia 'Project Offices' — restates COG function and links it to the Greenbrier
undercutting: AUTOVON switching alone fully accounts for a hardened, blast-valved, decontamination-equipped telephone building. DoD required its switches to survive; that requirement produces every observed feature without any sheltering function.
Helipads are D0 on the universal list where an aviation or medical justification is absent but a maintenance-access justification is present, which it is for remote mountaintops.
The claim's strongest form ('emergency relocation site for senior executive-branch officials') is asserted by no source I saw as anything other than a possibility.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This is the sharpest diagnosticity failure on the beat. Every physical signal offered for the COG reading — hardening, decontamination, helipad, security, generators — is REQUIRED by the AUTOVON mission on its own. A signal that both hypotheses predict at equal strength is D0 and contributes nothing at any volume. The Greenbrier switchboard label is the one genuine exception: a COG facility's own equipment naming this chain is improbable if the chain were purely a DoD voice-switching asset with no COG relationship. That single item is worth more than everything else in this row, and it is the item most worth receipting.

propositions.statement: The terminal stations of the chain (Hagerstown and Chatham) housed AUTOVON switching equipment for the Defense Communications Agency.
propositions.assessment: Consistently asserted across LaFrance, Wikipedia and CLUI, and consistent with the documented AUTOVON architecture (switches sited away from population centres, avoidance routing). No primary record seen. Conditional: an FCC ULS/ASR record establishes licensee and path but has authority only over the licence, not over the DoD network role, so it would be D4 for FUNCTION(relay) and no better than D2 for FUNCTION(AUTOVON switch). The record that would settle it is a DCA/DISA network document or a Bell System Practice.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net — 'The terminal stations contained AUTOVON switches'
Wikipedia 'Project Offices' — AUTOVON in service 1964, Chatham on line 1966
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Discriminates well against A07 'ordinary unhardened telecom exchange': an AUTOVON switch is a documented DoD asset class with a published architecture and published siting doctrine. It discriminates not at all against the COG reading, since AUTOVON and COG are compatible.

propositions.statement: The five stations enumerated here (Hagerstown MD / HGTWMDQ0010; Short Hill Mountain–Leesburg VA / LSBGVA05 / '[VA-1]'; Peters Mountain VA; Spears Mountain, Buckingham County VA; Chatham County NC) are the complete membership of the set the sources call 'Project Offices'.
propositions.assessment: Membership is asserted consistently but the boundary is soft. CLUI's Chatham entry calls Chatham 'the southernmost of four other facilities in the region', LaFrance calls Hagerstown 'the northernmost of five', and Peters Mountain and Buckingham are variously described as 'relay stations' between the Project Offices rather than as Project Offices themselves. Netcong NJ, which some search summaries associated with the group, is a different animal — AT&T's network operations centre, not a tropo station — and I have excluded it. The set is enumerable and closable, which matters: it is the precondition for the §9.2 C1c candidate-set path on any individual member.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net per-site pages naming Hagerstown as northernmost of five and Buckingham as part of the Project Office chain
CLUI Chatham entry — 'the southernmost of four other facilities in the region known as Project Offices'
undercutting: Terminology is inconsistent across sources: 'Project Office', 'troposcatter relay station' and 'Project Office chain' are used interchangeably, so the set may be a chain of five stations of two different classes rather than five instances of one class.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Not diagnostic of function; diagnostic of method. A closed set of five with a published denominator is what would let a thin instance be graded via C1c instead of being asserted at large. If the set is really 'two terminals plus three relays', N and M change and every member re-grades.

candidates.mundane_alternative: A07 — a hardened Defense Communications Agency AUTOVON switching and troposcatter relay chain and nothing more: a commercial carrier building military-grade voice plant under DoD contract, hardened because DoD's own specifications required survivable switching, with no sheltering or relocation role for any person. This null accounts for every physical feature reported: earth cover, blast valves, decontamination bay, standby generation, filtered positive-pressure ventilation, elevated physical security, remote siting. WHAT WOULD DISTINGUISH IT: berthing. A switching station houses equipment and a small maintenance crew; a relocation facility houses people. Bunk capacity, galley and messing provisions, potable-water storage sized to a population rather than to a crew, sanitary capacity, and a decontamination bay sized for personnel rather than vehicles all discriminate cleanly. Secondary discriminators: whether the parcel was ever federally leased or subject to a federal restrictive covenant (county deed chain); whether the site carries a federal frequency assignment in the NTIA GMF as well as an FCC licence; whether any DD-1391 or MILCON line names the location. All of these are checkable and none was checked in this sweep.
candidates.claim_origin: Two distinct origins, traced as far as the index allows. (1) THE FACTUAL SKELETON of the chain — five stations, their locations, tropo reflectors, earth-covered buildings, AUTOVON role — traces to Albert LaFrance, a named Virginia researcher, publishing at coldwar-c4i.net ('A Secret Landscape: The Cold War Infrastructure of the Nation's Capital Region'). The site has been running since at least the early 2000s; a 2002-era mailing-list post referencing it appears in the index, which is a usable earliest-appearance anchor but was not receipted. (2) THE COG INTERPRETATION traces to the same source, and — this is the important part — LaFrance states it as inference, in hedged language ('probably not the station's primary mission', 'most likely', 'may have served'). The unhedged form now circulating on Wikipedia, CLUI, Grokipedia, War History Online, OnlyInYourState and dozens of listicles is a downstream hardening of one researcher's stated conjecture. Separately, (3) the CHATHAM-SPECIFIC factual detail (purchase price, construction cost, contractor, square footage, 45-year operating span) traces to Jon Elliston, 'Big Hole, Deep Secret', Indy Week, 13 December 2000 — an independent origin, because Elliston appears to have worked from deed records and local interviews rather than from LaFrance. I could not establish an earlier appearance than 2000 for the Chatham material or than the early 2000s for the chain material, and I did not run the canonical ORIGIN corpora (Wayback CDX, IA full-text, Chronicling America), so no ORIGIN proposition is offered.
candidates.lineage_note: Not the many origins it appears to have. My best reading is THREE, possibly TWO. L1 = LaFrance / coldwar-c4i.net, from which Wikipedia's 'Project Offices' article, Grokipedia's mirror of it, Wikimapia annotations and most enthusiast restatements descend. L2 = CLUI's Land Use Database, whose entries read as independent site visits with independent photography, but whose framing language ('one of five similar facilities... known as Project Offices') is close enough to LaFrance's that under the §5.1.7 default — SAME under uncertainty — it should collapse into L1 until someone establishes CLUI's sourcing. L3 = Elliston / Indy Week 2000, genuinely independent for Chatham, since it predates most of the web corpus and works from local records and named interviews. Kastleman's 2020 Critical Military Studies article is a fourth publication but is a memoir-inflected scholarly treatment of the Chatham site and is likely downstream of Elliston and of family testimony rather than independent of both. NET: the COG claim has ONE lineage. The physical-description claim has at most two. CAP-1 would bind.
candidates.expected_records: For a 1960s programme built by a common carrier under federal contract, here is what SHOULD exist and whether the silence is surprising. COUNTY DEED AND ASSESSOR RECORDS FOR ALL FIVE PARCELS — X3, the universal floor; AT&T bought land in five named counties and those transfers are recorded. Their absence would be genuinely surprising and none has been checked. Elliston's reported $27,000 purchase price for the Chatham tract is exactly the sort of figure that comes out of a deed book, which is a reason to think the record exists and is findable. USGS HTMC TEMPORAL STACK — X3; five 1960s excavations on named landforms should appear, and editorial blanking between editions would itself be D2. FCC ASR/ULS — X3 for the towers as commercial emitters, though note the ASR is authoritative only for the structure and the licence, never for what is under it. NTIA GMF federal assignments — X0; federal spectrum is withheld by aggregation, and its absence carries no information at all. MILCON / DD-1391 — X0 if AT&T financed the buildings on its own capital, which is the ordinary Bell System pattern for Long Lines plant; X3 only if federal construction money flowed, and establishing which of those two worlds we are in is the single highest-value unresolved question on this beat. CREST / DTIC for a facility programme still partly operational — X0. NEPA — X0, predates NEPA entirely. FRPP / GSA disposal — X0, AT&T is not an executive agency. Bell System Practices and AT&T route/plant engineering literature — X2 and the best target: the Long Lines corporate record is partly in private and enthusiast hands and is the class of document that, per the calibration set's Fairview case, carries D3.
candidates.confidence_note: The chain's physical existence I regard as very likely true and well within reach of documentation; a county parcel sweep across five counties would probably settle EXIST at A or B within a day of unblocked access. The COG function I regard as genuinely open and currently ungraded in the strict sense — one researcher's hedged inference, restated confidently by everyone downstream, with a single genuinely diagnostic artefact (the Greenbrier switchboard label) that nobody appears to have pursued properly. The temptation on this beat is to let the chain's obvious realness launder the COG claim onto it. That is the v0.1 unit error and I have deliberately not made it.

candidates.name: AT&T Project Office, Short Hill Mountain, Loudoun County, Virginia
aliases: Project Aurelia (AT&T's internal name for the 2016 expansion, not for the site)
candidates.era: Underground facility built early 1960s (a county supervisor is quoted dating federal use to 1963); still AT&T-owned and operational; expansion sought and abandoned 2016; a monopole application refused 2021.

location.description: On the ridge of Short Hill Mountain in western Loudoun County, Virginia, in the 'Between the Hills' area near Hillsboro and Lovettsville, north of Harpers Ferry.
location.basis: Named landform from CLUI and Loudoun County land-use reporting. No coordinate resolved; the Loudoun County parcel record and the 2016 commission-permit file would both give an exact one and neither was reachable.

propositions.statement: A substantial subsurface structure exists on the ridge of Short Hill Mountain.
propositions.assessment: This is the strongest EXIST on the beat, for an unusual reason: in 2016 AT&T itself filed a land-use application with Loudoun County to build a 160,000 sq ft aboveground structure adjoining, in the reporting's words, 'its already-existing underground facility'. A corporation's own filing with a zoning authority, describing its own property, is a party with authority over the fact under §3.4(e), and the county is the record custodian. If CMPT-2016-0001 resolves and contains that description, this is a D4 row and EXIST reaches A on a single document. Conditional: A on the county file; B without it, on CLUI plus multiple bylined local-press accounts.
supporting: Loudoun County commission permit proceeding, reported application CMPT-2016-0001, 2016 — AT&T application to build adjacent to an existing underground facility
CLUI Land Use Database, AT&T Short Hill Mountain Site — underground bunker of at least several thousand square feet with a drive-in entrance
Loudoun Times-Mirror reporting, 'What's up there? There's more than meets the eye to Short Hill Mountain'
Loudoun Now reporting, June 2016, on the application's withdrawal
propositions.diagnosticity_note: The mundane null for Loudoun County — a data centre, in the county that is Data Center Alley — predicts an underground building poorly. Data centres in Loudoun are built at grade in commodity industrial shells. A 1960s earth-covered mountaintop structure is not what A07 produces. So EXIST is discriminating here in a way it usually is not.

propositions.statement: The subsurface structure is engineered against nuclear blast beyond ordinary construction for a telecommunications building.
propositions.assessment: Asserted by coldwar-c4i.net in the same terms as the rest of the chain — earth-covered, drive-through decontamination bay, blast-resistant microwave antennas, physical security beyond conventional AT&T practice. No instance-level engineering document seen. Conditional: this is where the beat's discipline bites hardest. Even a resolved county building-permit file is D2 at best for HARDEN unless it recites blast valves, shielding or a design standard on its face, exactly as the calibration set holds for Fairview: the licensing or permitting authority has authority over the permit, not over the hardening.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net [VA-1] page — earth-covered underground building, drive-through entrance-decontamination area, blast-resistant terrestrial microwave antennas
undercutting: No design standard, as-built, or specification naming this site was found. For a privately financed carrier building this is an X0/X1 silence and carries little weight, but it does mean the claim is one compiler deep.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A drive-through decontamination bay is the one reported feature that no mundane alternative for a mountaintop microwave station produces. Earth cover, generators, fuel and security are all D0. If the decontamination bay can be evidenced from a filed drawing or a georeferenced photograph by a resolvable observer, HARDEN moves; without it, HARDEN is a restatement of the chain-level claim.

propositions.statement: The site is owned and operated by AT&T, and has hosted a federal government activity since approximately 1963.
propositions.assessment: AT&T ownership is not in dispute and is trivially checkable in the Loudoun parcel record. The federal-activity half rests on one on-the-record statement: Supervisor Geary Higgins (R-Catoctin), quoted in the Loudoun Times-Mirror, saying 'This is and has been a government site up there since 1963.' Under §5.4 he passes the identity gate comfortably — an elected county supervisor is resolvable in records created for entirely unrelated purposes and predating the claim — and attestation custody is satisfied by a bylined quotation in named local press. He fails the position-to-know clause: nothing places a county supervisor in a role that would give him authority over what a classified tenant does on a mountaintop. His statement is therefore a resolvable named person's belief, not a knowledgeable account, and it enters at low diagnosticity. Conditional: CONTROL(AT&T) reaches A on the parcel record; CONTROL(federal activity) is capped at E by CAP-2b on the current record.

Loudoun Times-Mirror — AT&T invoked a confidentiality clause regarding the 2016 project, internally 'Project Aurelia'
Reporting that visitors to the site require a background check
undercutting: A background-check requirement for site access is standard for critical carrier infrastructure and for any facility carrying government traffic under contract; it does not require a federal tenant.
A confidentiality clause in a commercial land-use filing is ordinary corporate practice for network plant and is equally consistent with a competitively sensitive data-centre build.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Higgins's statement is the only claim-property item here — it is about the claim (a government site), not about the place. Everything else (security, confidentiality, background checks) is place-property and D0 against A07. That asymmetry is precisely what CAP-2b measures, and it is why a site this visibly interesting still cannot carry a CONTROL(federal) grade.

propositions.statement: The 2016 'Project Aurelia' proposal specified a 160,000 sq ft, 35 ft tall aboveground structure with eight 4 MW standby generators, a large cooling plant, roughly 2 million gallons of water annually, and about 60 staff on a 24/7 basis.
propositions.assessment: This is the single most quantitatively specific thing on the whole beat and it comes from a public county land-use file, which is the best custody available to me. The numbers are internally coherent and, read together, they are a data-centre profile: roughly 32 MW of standby generation against 160,000 sq ft and 60 staff is on the order of 200 W/sq ft, which is IT load, not office load. Conditional: if the county file resolves, this is D4 for FEATURE and D3 as an UNDERCUTS row against the COG reading of the 2016 expansion, because the null predicts it far better than the proposition does.
supporting: Loudoun County commission permit file as reported by Loudoun Times-Mirror, Loudoun Now, Piedmont Environmental Council, Friends of the Blue Ridge Mountains, and Data Center Dynamics

propositions.diagnosticity_note: This row cuts AGAINST the interesting hypothesis and that is why it belongs here. A 32 MW standby plant and a 2-million-gallon annual water draw are what a hyperscale or carrier data centre needs; they are not what a hardened relocation facility needs, and they are radically disproportionate to a 1960s tropo station's load. The register should record that the most specific, best-custodied document on this site points at the mundane explanation for the 2016 works. candidates.mundane_alternative: A07 — an AT&T long-haul microwave and switching station, hardened in the 1960s to DoD's AUTOVON survivability specification, which since divestiture has become an ordinary piece of AT&T network real estate and which in 2016 the company wanted to expand into a conventional carrier data centre, on a mountaintop it already owned, in the county that hosts more data-centre capacity than anywhere on earth. I found no appearance of the Chatham material earlier than 2000 in the index, but I did NOT run the canonical ORIGIN corpora — no Wayback CDX, no IA full-text, no Chronicling America sweep of Chatham County and Durham papers from 1960–1968, which is where a construction-era local story would live. propositions.statement: Albemarle County building permits issued to AT&T record approximately $61 million of works at the site in 2007.
propositions.assessment: IF TRUE, this is the single most diagnostic quantitative fact I encountered on the beat. Sixty-one million dollars of permitted work at a mountaintop microwave relay whose troposcatter mission had ended is grossly disproportionate to the building class, and permit valuation far above class norm is a catalogued D3 signal for the urban/in-building profile and behaves the same way here. It is also, critically, a T1 county record with a public machine-accessible index — Albemarle County operates a building-permit document viewer. BUT: I could not trace this claim to a permit number, an application, or any document. Its visible origin is the Wikipedia 'Project Offices' article citing 'Albemarle County building permits'. That is a claim ABOUT a record, not a record. Conditional: if a permit resolves at the county with that valuation, this is D3 and moves the entry materially; if it does not, this is an untraced number circulating on a wiki and should be recorded as such.
supporting: Wikipedia 'Project Offices', citing Albemarle County building permits — $61 million of updates in 2007
undercutting: No permit number, date or applicant name accompanies the figure in any source I saw.

Large carrier capital projects at existing sites are routine; $61M is extraordinary for a relay hut but not for a core network node or a substantial data-hall build, so even if confirmed it is consistent with the commercial null at the upper end.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This is the beat's clearest illustration of why a number needs a receipt. The figure, if real, is high-diagnosticity and cheap to check at a named authority with a public index; unverified, it is exactly the kind of specific, plausible, unsourced quantity that propagates and that this register exists to catch. I am recording it as a lead with its acquisition path named, not as support.

propositions.statement: The site relayed AUTOVON traffic by troposcatter between the Project Offices at Leesburg (Short Hill Mountain) and Hagerstown to the north and Lynchburg to the south.

supporting: coldwar-c4i.net — relay station in the Project Office tropo chain, northward link to Hagerstown, southern link to Lynchburg
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Falsifiable topology, uncheck. Surviving reflector azimuths and FCC path records would settle it.

candidates.name: AT&T "Buckingham" troposcatter relay station, Spears Mountain, Buckingham County, Virginia
candidates.era: Reported built late 1950s; closed early 2000s; subsurface portion reportedly sold to private interests and used for storage; surface reportedly sold to private homeowners; concrete tropo reflectors reportedly still standing.

location.description: Atop Spears Mountain, roughly 11 miles west of the town of Buckingham, Buckingham County, Virginia, near the geographic centre of the state.
location.basis: Named mountain, county and distance-from-town, from coldwar-c4i.net and CLUI via search summaries. No coordinate resolved.

propositions.statement: A nuclear-hardened subsurface structure and large concrete parabolic troposcatter reflectors exist on Spears Mountain.
propositions.assessment: Asserted by coldwar-c4i.net, CLUI, and a local television news piece ('The Mystery of Spears Mountain', WSET). The reflectors are described as still standing, which makes this the most externally verifiable EXIST in the chain — a large concrete paraboloid is unmistakable in imagery and unmistakable from a public road. Conditional: EXIST plausibly reaches A via the A1-alt direct-observation path if two resolvable named observers with lawful access produce georeferenced imagery, plus a Buckingham County parcel record. That is a realistic near-term target because the property is now privately held and partly residential.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net Buckingham page
CLUI Land Use Database, Buckingham AT&T Relay Site
WSET (Lynchburg) — 'The Mystery of Spears Mountain'
Cryptome 'eyeball' page on an unknown facility on White Rock Road
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Concrete billboard-type tropo reflectors are genuinely diagnostic of a specific technology and era in a way that a hole is not — troposcatter is not something a limestone mine, a water works or a commercial data centre produces. This is one of the few place-property signals on the beat that actually discriminates, because it is a technology signature rather than an infrastructure signature.

propositions.statement: The station was not part of AT&T's commercial long-distance network and existed solely to provide national-security communications on AUTOVON, linking Washington-area command centres to Fort Bragg, Pope AFB and Seymour Johnson AFB.
propositions.assessment: This is a strong, specific, exclusive claim — 'not part of the commercial network' — and it is single-sourced to LaFrance. It is also the most checkable functional claim on the beat, because its negation is checkable: if the site appears in AT&T's commercial route and plant literature or in commercial FCC path licences, the exclusivity claim fails. Conditional: E to D on the current record; C or better only with a route record or an FCC licence set.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net Buckingham page — 'existed solely to provide national-security communications'
undercutting: None found, but see the diagnosticity note: the absence of a commercial-route listing has not been established, only asserted.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: An exclusivity claim is a negative claim and requires a completed, receipted negative search across the commercial route corpus — the Long Lines route literature and the FCC licence record — to have any weight at all. LaFrance may well have done that work; I have no way to know from a search summary, and the register cannot credit unseen diligence.

propositions.statement: The facility is closed, in private ownership, with the subsurface space used for storage and the surface in residential use.
propositions.assessment: This is the calibration set's R-02 shape in miniature and it matters: private residential occupancy and commercial storage use are affirmative UNDERCUTS against any current federal-facility reading, at meaningful magnitude, because they are improbable if the proposition were true. They do NOT undercut the historical FUNCTION claim. Conditional: with a resolved deed, this supports a clean STATUS(converted) and simultaneously an UNDERCUTS row on any present-tense COG claim.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net — closed early 2000s, sold to private interests, storage use, topside sold to private homeowners
CLUI — now privately owned and part of a residence
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Residential occupancy of a claimed hardened federal facility is an E0/A3 cell — very improbable under the proposition, entirely expected under the null — and would generate a genuine negative row. The register should carry it as such rather than quietly dropping a fact that cuts against the interesting story.

candidates.mundane_alternative: A07 / A12 — a decommissioned AT&T troposcatter relay of a well-documented Cold War type, obsolete, sold off, and now a private house with a very unusual basement. WHAT WOULD DISTINGUISH IT from a facility with a continuing role: the deed chain and current assessment record, both public in Buckingham County, plus the simple fact that a residence and a classified facility cannot occupy the same footprint. Here the mundane alternative is probably the truth about the present, and the live question is only about 1958–2000.
candidates.claim_origin: Albert LaFrance, coldwar-c4i.net, Buckingham page; CLUI parallel entry; Wikimapia annotation. Independently, WSET (ABC affiliate, Lynchburg) produced a local news segment, 'The Mystery of Spears Mountain', which is a separate origin for local awareness though I could not date it or determine its sourcing. Cryptome hosts an 'eyeball' page on a facility on White Rock Road which may or may not be the same object — I could not establish identity and have not assumed it.
candidates.lineage_note: One documentary lineage (LaFrance, with CLUI collapsing into it under the default) plus one broadcast lineage (WSET) of unknown depth. The Cryptome page is a possible third but its subject identity is unestablished and under §11.1 coordinate or road-name proximity flags, never merges.

This is the cheapest high-value acquisition on the entire beat. USGS HTMC — X3. FCC ASR — X3, including any dismantle record. VIRGINIA DHR / architectural survey — X1. MILCON/FRPP/GSA — X0. CREST/DTIC — X2 if the programme is declassified, X0 otherwise.
candidates.confidence_note: Modest evidence, but the highest verification-yield-per-effort of any candidate here, because the property changed hands recently and into private hands, which forces a recorded transaction. A single deed pull would move three propositions at once.

candidates.name: AT&T Netcong underground network operations centre, New Jersey — now the Roxbury Vault
candidates.era: Announced 1968; principal AT&T network operations centre for over a decade; sold to Vital Records Incorporated in 1995; operating as a records-storage and tape-vaulting facility with a data centre inside.
candidates.jurisdiction: Morris County, New Jersey (Netcong borough / Roxbury township area)

location.description: On a hilltop in or adjoining Netcong borough, Morris County, New Jersey, in the general area of AT&T's later Bedminster and Basking Ridge centres.
location.basis: Borough name from CLUI and from the operator's own facility page. No coordinate resolved. Note the naming conflict: CLUI calls it Netcong, the operator calls it Roxbury — adjoining municipalities — which is itself an entity-resolution hazard worth recording.

propositions.statement: A two-level subsurface structure exists at the site.
propositions.assessment: About as solid as anything gets short of a receipt: a currently operating commercial business publishes the building as its product and invites customers into it, CLUI has visited, and a 1968 construction announcement is referenced. Conditional: A is realistic once the Morris County deed recording the 1995 AT&T-to-VRI sale and the borough or township assessment record resolve. Both should exist and both should be findable — a 1995 commercial transfer is inside the digitisation window for most New Jersey jurisdictions.
supporting: CLUI Land Use Database, Netcong Bunker
Vital Records Inc. own facility page for the Roxbury vault
Reference to a 1968 AT&T announcement of a two-storey building at the bottom of a 47-foot hole
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Existence is uncontested by anyone, including the current owner, so the diagnosticity question barely arises. The interesting propositions here are EXTENT and HARDEN.

propositions.statement: The structure is two levels, at approximately 30 and 50 feet below grade, of between 86,000 and 125,000 square feet.
propositions.assessment: There is a live and specific quantitative conflict here that nobody appears to have noticed. CLUI says 86,000 square feet. The operator says more than 125,000 square feet of usable space across two floors at 30 and 50 feet. A 45 per cent discrepancy between an independent surveyor and the owner is not noise. The likeliest reconciliation is that the figures measure different things (gross structure versus usable including mezzanine or added build-out since 1995) but that is my inference, not a finding. Conditional: D until an assessment record, a filed floor plan or a fire-code occupancy filing resolves it — the KUMMSC pattern again.
supporting: CLUI — 86,000 sq ft, two levels, concrete walls more than 2 feet thick, entirely cased in steel
Vital Records Inc. — two underground floors at 30 and 50 feet below ground, more than 125,000 sq ft usable
undercutting: The two figures contradict each other and one of them is self-published by a party selling space by the square foot, which is a commercial incentive to state the larger number.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Not about hardening at all — about whether the register can carry a number. The operator's figure is SELF-PUBLISHED and under §2.4 is excluded from V outright, which means on the current record the only admissible figure is CLUI's, and CLUI's is unsourced. That is the honest position and it is more useful than splitting the difference.

propositions.diagnosticity_note: A complete steel envelope is E3/A0-ish against A07 — an ordinary telephone exchange or commercial records warehouse is not cased in steel, because the only reason to do it is electromagnetic shielding. Getting the underlying Bell System document once fixes the whole class; getting it never means the whole class sits at C forever, correctly.

propositions.statement: The structure is three-foot reinforced concrete, more than 50 feet underground, and was designed to survive a 20-megaton nuclear detonation at 2.5 miles.
propositions.assessment: This is the beat's cleanest §2.5 case and I want to set it out carefully. Every quantitative hardening figure in circulation for this building comes from the operator's own marketing, reproduced verbatim by data-centre directories, listicles and trade blogs. The operator is the party advancing the claim and the claim is the product; the material is SELF-PUBLISHED and, for the hardening proposition specifically, self-attesting. Under §2.4 it is excluded from V entirely. Worse, the '20 megaton at 2.5 miles' figure is not a measurement of this building at all: it is a NETWORK-WIDE AT&T design assumption for one hardness class, documented at the programme level, transposed onto an individual instance. That is the CLASS-to-INSTANCE error §2.4 exists to block. Conditional: with the operator's material excluded, V for HARDEN is empty and this proposition would sit at F, not D — it is not that the evidence is weak, it is that there is no admissible evidence at all.
undercutting: The '20 megaton at 2.5 miles / 1000 mph wind / 40 G' figures are a programme-level AT&T design criterion, not an instance specification, and applying them here is unsupported.

The operator's description of the site as 'a former Government Command Bunker... purpose-built by the military' is contradicted by every independent account, all of which attribute construction to AT&T Long Lines.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Marketing copy about a building's blast rating discriminates nothing, because the null — an ordinary commercial data centre in a genuinely old, genuinely thick concrete building — predicts exactly the same copy. Operators of converted bunkers have a direct commercial incentive to state the strongest available hardening claim, which makes their assertions anti-diagnostic: the more dramatic the number, the more it is explained by the sales motive.

The site-history material is a second lineage (CLUI / Long Lines corpus). A third, Wikimapia, is CROWD-EDITED and contributes a lead only. candidates.name: Western Union "Tenley Tower" microwave radio terminal, Tenleytown, Washington DC — and the Washington Area Wideband System
aliases: Western Union Telegraph Company Washington Radio Terminal
Western Union Telegraph Company Tenley Site
candidates.era: Built 1945–1947 as a commercial microwave terminal; reported repurposed in the late 1970s as a repeater in the Washington Area Wideband System; now a commercial cell site owned by a tower-leasing company.

location.description: In the Tenleytown neighbourhood of northwest Washington DC, near the highest natural elevation in the District, in the vicinity of 41st Street NW and Wisconsin Avenue. One search summary gives a street address of 4623 41st Street NW.
location.basis: Neighbourhood and street address from search summaries of DC Historic Sites and coldwar-c4i.net. The address was not resolved and one search summary explicitly corrected a different address I had proposed, so treat it as indicative. No coordinate asserted.

propositions.statement: A 1945–47 cast-concrete microwave terminal building with an attached octagonal tower, approximately 73 feet tall, exists at the site.
propositions.assessment: This is the only candidate on the beat with a plausible route to a genuine T1 primary: the building and tower are reported listed on the National Register of Historic Places and are carried by DC Historic Sites (DC Preservation League). An NRHP nomination is a T1/T2 document, machine-resolvable through NPS, that describes construction, dimensions, materials, architect and history on its face. Conditional: A on the nomination alone, once reachable. This is also the only candidate where the architect is named — Leon Chatelain Jr. — which opens an architectural-records lineage entirely independent of the Cold War literature.
supporting: DC Historic Sites (DC Preservation League) entry — 73-foot octagonal transmission tower built 1945–1947 near the city's highest elevation, designed by Leon Chatelain Jr.

Rotenstein, 'Towers for Telegrams: The Western Union Telegraph Company and the Emergence of Microwave Telecommunications Infrastructure', IA: The Journal of the Society for Industrial Archeology 32(2), 2006
coldwar-c4i.net Western Union Tenleytown page
Public photography by named photographers including Matt Blaze
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Existence is trivially established and uninteresting. The candidate earns its place for a different reason: it is the one place on this beat where a peer-reviewed industrial-archaeology article and a heritage nomination provide a documentary standard the rest of the beat lacks, and it therefore sets the bar.

propositions.statement: The tower served as a node in Western Union's Washington Area Wideband System, a Department of Defense redundant data and video network of coaxial and 6 GHz microwave links, connecting facilities including the Naval Security Station, NSA's Friendship Annex, Andrews AFB, Liberty Dam, and the Alternate Joint Communications Center at Blue Ridge Summit.
propositions.assessment: This is the most valuable and least-known thing I found on this beat. WAWS is a named, acronymed DoD system with a documented node list, and it is a Western Union rather than AT&T network — a whole hardened-communications lineage largely absent from the Long Lines-dominated literature. Its endpoints are named, acknowledged federal installations, which makes the topology checkable. The claim originates with LaFrance's WAWS pages and route map. Conditional: WAWS as a PROGRAM is a strong candidate for B or better once DoD/DCA documentation is searched, because unlike 'Project Offices' it has an acronym that will appear in indexes.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net WAWS index and WAWS microwave route map
coldwar-c4i.net Tenleytown page — repurposed in the late 1970s as a WAWS repeater
Rotenstein 2006 on Western Union's national-security communications role
undercutting: The Tenleytown building itself is an above-ground 1947 commercial structure and nothing suggests it was hardened. A node in a defence network is not thereby a bunker, and this candidate is included as a comms-relay, not as a hardened facility.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A named system acronym is disproportionately diagnostic in this domain because it is a search key that reaches indexed federal corpora. 'WAWS' is the kind of term that appears in DCA/DISA histories, in GAO reports and in appropriations language, where 'Project Office' does not. The highest-value follow-up on this entire beat may be a systematic WAWS search across GovInfo, DTIC and NARA.

propositions.statement: The Tenleytown terminal was hardened beyond ordinary construction.
propositions.assessment: No source claims this and I am recording the proposition specifically in order to record its absence. A cast-concrete 1947 building near a city's high point is a microwave terminal, not a bunker, and the register should hold a node of a national-security network at D or below on hardening unless something says otherwise. Conditional: this is a case where an expected record IS informative — an NRHP nomination describes construction in detail, so a nomination that does not mention protective engineering is a genuine, if mild, UNDERCUTS row rather than a silence.
undercutting: An NRHP nomination, if it resolves, would be a detailed architectural description by a party with authority over the historic record; its silence on hardening would be informative in a way most silences on this beat are not.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This row exists to make a point the beat needs: participation in a defence network is not hardening, and the two propositions must not be allowed to borrow from each other. The Tenleytown tower is a case where FUNCTION is interesting and HARDEN is almost certainly negative.

supporting: coldwar-c4i.net — owned by a tower-site leasing firm, American Tower Corporation, now a cellular cell site
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Present commercial tower ownership is an affirmative UNDERCUTS against any current national-security-facility reading — a leased commercial cell site with a public ASR registration is the opposite of a covert asset.

candidates.mundane_alternative: A07 — a pioneering 1947 commercial microwave terminal, architecturally notable, which like most surviving microwave real estate carried government traffic under contract during the Cold War and is now a cell site. WHAT WOULD DISTINGUISH IT from something more: nothing found suggests anything more about the building. The interesting object here is not the building but the NETWORK, and the register should be careful not to let an architecturally distinctive tower stand in for a system it merely touched.
candidates.claim_origin: Three genuinely separate origins, which is unusual for this beat. (1) The architectural and historical record originates with the heritage documentation — DC Historic Sites / DC Preservation League and, behind it, the NRHP nomination, plus Tenleytown local history material. (2) The scholarly account of Western Union's microwave network originates with David S. Rotenstein, 'Towers for Telegrams', IA: The Journal of the Society for Industrial Archeology 32(2), 2006, with related material on his blog (historian4hire) including a Western Union microwave network survey and a 2010 piece on continuity-of-government sites as recent-past resources. (3) The WAWS material and the node list originate with Albert LaFrance, coldwar-c4i.net. These three do not descend from one another.
candidates.lineage_note: Three, which is the most on this beat, and they are independent under the access test: a heritage nomination, a peer-reviewed industrial archaeologist working from Western Union corporate records, and a Cold War infrastructure researcher working from network documentation could each have produced their account without the others. Rotenstein is a professional historian with a byline and a citable venue, which also makes him the highest-tier secondary source I encountered on this beat.
candidates.expected_records: NRHP NOMINATION — X3 and reachable through NPS; the single highest-value document for this candidate and a genuine T1/T2 primary. DC HISTORIC PRESERVATION OFFICE landmark file — X3. DC RECORDER OF DEEDS — X3, universal floor. FCC ASR AND ULS — X3, ownership and licence history for a registered structure in continuous commercial use. DCA/DISA AND DoD DOCUMENTATION MENTIONING 'WAWS' — X1 to X2 and completely unexplored; a system with an acronym and a node list including NSA and AJCC endpoints should leave traces in GovInfo, DTIC and NARA finding aids. WESTERN UNION CORPORATE RECORDS — X2; Rotenstein evidently reached some. MILCON — X0, Western Union is not an appropriated entity, which is the Mount Pony blind-spot pattern exactly and should be flagged on the entry.
candidates.confidence_note: I am including this candidate less for the tower than for WAWS. The register's Long Lines material will be AT&T-shaped by default because that is where the enthusiast literature is; Western Union ran a parallel hardened government network that is barely represented anywhere, has a named acronym that will index well, and has a serious scholarly treatment already in print. If one thread from this sweep is worth a dedicated follow-up cycle, it is this one.

candidates.name: AT&T Long Lines unmanned microwave repeater sites, Missouri (Brinktown, Dover, Slater, Lawrenceton, Windsor, Hermann, Prairie Home)
candidates.era: Constructed 1953 to circa 1964 as unmanned microwave repeaters on Kansas City–St Louis and Kansas City–east routes; used through the 1980s; variously abandoned, sold, or converted to public-safety radio use.
candidates.jurisdiction: Multiple Missouri counties, including Maries County (Brinktown), Lafayette County (Dover), Saline County (Slater), Ste. Genevieve County (Lawrenceton)

location.description: Rural sites across central and eastern Missouri along the AT&T Long Lines Kansas City–St Louis and Kansas City–east microwave routes, each identified in the underlying source by an FCC Antenna Structure Registration number and by named township.
location.basis: Named towns and counties from search summaries of Garrett Fuller's site-by-site blog. No coordinates resolved. Note that FCC ASR records carry surveyed coordinates for every registered structure, which makes this the one candidate class on the beat where exact locations are cheaply and authoritatively obtainable — from a corpus I could not reach.

propositions.statement: Registered antenna structures and associated equipment buildings exist at these locations.
propositions.assessment: Effectively certain and, uniquely on this beat, tied to specific federal identifiers: ASR 1005484 (Brinktown), ASR 1010168 (Dover), ASR 1005501 (Lawrenceton). These are FCC registrations of physical structures by a licensing authority with authority over the registration. Conditional: A on the ASR record alone, which is a T1 machine-resolvable source with surveyed coordinates and construction dates. I MUST REPEAT: I did not resolve these numbers and they reached me through a search summary of a personal blog. They are leads.
supporting: Garrett Fuller, personal.garrettfuller.org, per-site pages for Missouri Long Lines sites, reportedly citing FCC records including ASR numbers and construction dates
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A registered tower is an entirely mundane object and the ASR proves only the structure. Its diagnostic value is negative and that is the point of this entry: it establishes the baseline against which the hardened sites must be distinguished.

propositions.statement: These sites are hardened facilities.
propositions.assessment: This proposition is stated in order to be answered NO, and that is the entry's purpose. These are unmanned repeater huts — small buildings on rural land with a tower, built to relay telephone and television traffic. Nothing in the source material claims hardening for them. The great majority of the several hundred Long Lines sites in the United States are of this class, not of the Lyons or Fairview class, and a register that ingests the Long Lines corpus without that distinction will manufacture hundreds of spurious hardened facilities out of ordinary telephone plant. Conditional: this proposition should grade at F or R, not at D — there is no admissible support and, unlike a classified facility, the silence here IS informative, because an unmanned rural repeater has no expected-record profile that would conceal hardening.
undercutting: Sites described as unmanned remote repeaters, which is structurally incompatible with the crew accommodation, life support and blast provisions that define the hardened main-station class.
Lawrenceton is now owned by the State of Missouri and used for the MOSWIN public-safety radio network — documented, benign, continuous public-agency occupancy.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: The most important diagnosticity statement on this beat: 'AT&T Long Lines site' does NOT imply 'hardened site'. Over a hundred main stations were hardened; roughly a thousand repeater vaults were built to a much lower standard; and the unmanned microwave repeaters were not hardened at all. Three tiers, one corpus, one name. Every hardening claim must be attached to a specific site's specific class, and the popular literature routinely attaches the main-station specifications to whatever site it happens to be describing.

propositions.statement: These were unmanned microwave repeater sites relaying telephone and television traffic on AT&T Long Lines' Kansas City–St Louis and Kansas City–east routes, and are not command, switching or continuity facilities.
propositions.assessment: Supported by the per-site research and consistent with the documented Long Lines network architecture, in which a small number of manned main stations are separated by long chains of unmanned repeaters. Conditional: FUNCTION(commercial microwave repeater) is an A target on FCC ULS path licences, which name the licensee, the path endpoints, the frequencies and the emission — a licensing authority with authority over exactly that fact, which is the §3.4(e) condition satisfied cleanly. This is the one FUNCTION proposition on the whole beat with a straightforward route to D4, and it is the boring one.
supporting: Garrett Fuller, per-site pages describing Brinktown as the sixth hop east of Kansas City on a telephone/television microwave route, and Slater as an unmanned remote repeater between Kansas City and St Louis
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Fully discriminating against every interesting hypothesis, which is the point. A licensed commercial microwave path with named endpoints and a published emission designator is what an ordinary telephone relay looks like in the record, and it looks nothing like a hardened facility. Establishing what the mundane case looks like in the FCC record is the prerequisite for claiming that some other site does not look like it.

propositions.statement: Ownership has passed variously from AT&T to private parties, tower companies, and in at least one case to the State of Missouri for public-safety radio.
propositions.assessment: Supported by the underlying blog's per-site FCC and ownership research. Conditional: settled by ASR ownership records, which are current and authoritative.
supporting: Lawrenceton (ASR 1005501) reported owned by the State of Missouri for MOSWIN
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Documented public-agency ownership for an unrelated purpose is an affirmative negative against any covert reading — the SubTropolis pattern applied to towers.

candidates.mundane_alternative: A07, and in this case the mundane alternative is almost certainly simply the truth: unmanned commercial microwave repeaters on a telephone company's long-haul route, of which several hundred were built, most now derelict, sold, or repurposed for cellular and public-safety radio. WHAT WOULD DISTINGUISH a hardened site from these: a subsurface structure at all; crew accommodation; blast doors; filtered positive-pressure ventilation; a decontamination provision; and a place on the L-carrier main-station list rather than on the repeater list. Those are bright lines and they are documented in the corpus itself.
candidates.claim_origin: Garrett Fuller, personal.garrettfuller.org, a per-site enthusiast survey covering Missouri Long Lines sites which — unusually and creditably — cites FCC records site by site. The source registry identifies this as P4 and as a backward-sourcing target, which is right: the value is that it names identifiers a researcher can independently resolve, not that its own assertions carry weight. This is the transparent-compiler pattern under §5.1.3: if the FCC records resolve, the FCC is the lineage and Fuller scores nothing, which is exactly as it should be and is not a criticism of him.
candidates.lineage_note: One compiler exposing what appear to be genuinely independent federal primaries. If the ASR numbers resolve, each site's EXIST rests on the FCC and there is no compiler lineage at all. If they do not resolve, there is one T4 terminus and three confabulation events to record.
candidates.expected_records: FCC ASR — X3, definitively; every registered structure over 200 feet or near an airport is in the database with surveyed coordinates, owner history and construction date. FCC ULS microwave path licences — X3 for the historic routes; the COMSEARCH path data sheets and engineering exhibits filed as ULS application attachments are, per the source registry, public, online and apparently never bulk-harvested. COUNTY DEED AND ASSESSOR in each county — X3. MISSOURI STATE PROPERTY RECORD for the Lawrenceton MOSWIN site — X2. USGS HTMC — X3. MILCON/FRPP/CREST/DTIC — X0 throughout; these are private commercial structures and no federal record class applies.
candidates.confidence_note: This is the beat's negative control and I have included it deliberately, in the spirit of the calibration set's Fairview/SubTropolis pairing. The register will be judged partly on whether it can hold an AT&T Long Lines hardened main station and an AT&T Long Lines unmanned repeater hut apart, given that they share a corporate parent, a network name, a decade, a rural setting, a tower and an enthusiast literature. On place-signals they are hard to separate; on documentation they are trivially separable, and the register should separate them on documentation.
